content.p: On the evening of Tuesday 28 June 2011, gunmen and suicide bombers forced their way into the Inter-Continental Hotel in Kabul. The hotel, on a hill above the city, was a favourite stopping point for Westerners, diplomats and Afghan officials. The attack ran for about five hours and ended only after NATO helicopters fired on the roof, where the last attackers had taken up positions. The Taliban claimed responsibility. The number of people killed is disputed: the Interior Ministry and the press gave figures from seven to 21, and the reports differ on who was counted.

The Inter-Continental was built in the 1960s and was, according to RFE/RL, the nation's first international luxury hotel. It had at least 200 rooms. It stood on a hill that overlooked the city, and Al Jazeera reported that it had not been part of the InterContinental hotel chain since 1980. For years it had been one of the places where foreigners and government officials met, stayed and held conferences.

Visitors had to pass several checkpoints on a winding road to reach it. Al Jazeera's correspondent Bernard Smith, reporting from Kabul, said it was "relatively easy" to get onto the premises despite four separate security checks on the road, The Afghan National Security Directorate spokesman, Luftullah Mashal, told VOA that the attackers may have taken advantage of a gap in security. "There was a loophole in the security, definitely," he said.

The attack came at a politically sensitive moment. Hours earlier, American, Pakistani and Afghan officials had met in Kabul to discuss prospects for peace talks with the Taliban, according to RFE/RL. A conference on the transition of security to Afghan forces was due to open at the hotel the next day, and many provincial governors and officials were staying there. NATO had agreed to move its forces out of combat roles by 2014, and Afghan forces were due to take control of more areas in July.

Violence had also risen after US forces killed Osama bin Laden on 2 May, and the Taliban had begun their spring offensive. Two earlier attacks in Kabul shaped the mood. On 18 June, gunmen in Afghan army uniforms attacked a police station close to the presidential palace and killed nine officers. In late May, a suicide bomber in an Afghan police uniform had infiltrated the main military hospital and killed six medical students, RFE/RL reported. VOA noted that the last major attack on a Kabul hotel had been in 2008, when militants stormed the Serena Hotel in the city centre and killed eight people.

ABC News reported that the attack began while guests were having dinner, and that power to the hotel and the surrounding neighbourhood had been cut. Nazir Amini, an Afghan visiting from Germany, told the Sydney Morning Herald that he had just returned from the buffet with a bowl of ice cream when two men carrying an AK-47 and a machinegun came out and began shooting at guests seated around the pool. Women and children screamed, chairs tipped over and people ran.

A receptionist told Reuters, as reported by Al Jazeera, that after several explosions the attackers went into the building and made their way to the ballroom. Some carried tape recorders playing Taliban war songs and fired at anyone they saw. Guests jumped from the second and third floors to escape. A hotel manager on duty told Al Jazeera that the hotel's cameras showed nine attackers had entered.The Interior Ministry's security officer Samoonyar Mohammad Zaman told Al Jazeera that there were 60 to 70 guests in the hotel that night.

ABC News reported that a suicide bomber detonated at the entrance, and that gunfire was accompanied by at least four explosions. Afghan police fought the attackers while commandos arrived later. ABC News quoted Afghan Interior Minister Bismillah Khan Mohammadi saying six attackers were dead, though one more could still be hiding in the building. Afghan commandos and international forces regained control of the hotel about four hours after it was stormed, ABC reported.

The BBC reported that three attackers reached the roof, and that Afghan officials then called on ISAF, the NATO-led force, for help. NATO helicopters circling over the hotel fired rockets that killed three insurgents on the roof, ABC News reported. Al Jazeera said that two of the helicopters fired on them. ISAF spokesman Major Tim James told AFP, as the BBC reported, that those killed on the roof appeared to have been wearing suicide vests, and that the explosions there may have been caused either by the attackers detonating themselves or by the helicopter fire.

NATO's account of its role differed in emphasis. Its spokesman, Master Sergeant Jason Haag, told VOA that coalition forces had been mobilised at the request of the Afghan Interior Ministry, that the response was mostly "an Afghan-led operation", and that the coalition's contribution was air support plus ISAF mentors who were part of the Afghan unit. The BBC reported that two New Zealand members of ISAF special forces were moderately injured. A New Zealand Defence Force statement released in 2017 said that a corporal who had served in the attack was wounded by grenade and rifle fire, and rescued guests from the hotel as fire broke out. The statement added that he had been awarded the New Zealand Gallantry Star in 2014 for his service in Afghanistan, including the incident at the hotel.

The fighting did not end cleanly. The BBC, citing Kabul police chief Gen. Ayoub Salangi, said one attacker had stayed alive by concealing himself in a hotel room. He set off his vest at about 0700 local time, after the fighting was thought to be over. The blast killed two policemen and a Spanish guest, and injured three others. Spain's foreign ministry later confirmed the death of a Spanish citizen and said he was an airline pilot. Salangi said the man had gone back to his room although security forces had advised against it.

Guests and officials also questioned the police response. The Sydney Morning Herald quoted Maulavi Mohammadullah Rusgi, chairman of the Takhar provincial council, who was at dinner when the attack started and said three of his friends were killed. He said that even after shooting stopped at about 5 a.m., police were reluctant to enter the hotel despite orders from Salangi. Other witnesses said police had run away or refused to shoot. A Western official quoted by the same newspaper said the Afghan police had "acquitted themselves pretty well", adding that "it could have been a whole lot worse."

The early figures were low and rose over the following days, and the sources did not agree. RFE/RL's first report, from the morning after, said the attack had left seven Afghan civilians dead and eight others wounded, including two police. The Interior Ministry spokesman, Sediq Sediqqi, told Al Jazeera on 29 June that there were 10 victims, eight civilians and two police officers. The BBC gave a different breakdown the same day: six more attackers, two police and 11 civilians, including a Spaniard. VOA reported 11 civilians and police dead in addition to the attackers.

The total on the attackers' side also differed. Sediqqi told Al Jazeera that all eight suicide bombers had been killed, while RFE/RL quoted him saying six had attacked. The Sydney Morning Herald's report said at least 21 people had died in the attack, including nine suicide bombers. The Long War Journal put the toll at 12. Looking back in January 2018, RFE/RL described the June 2011 attack as having killed 21 people, at least 10 of them civilians.

The Taliban spokesman, Zabiullah Mujahid, claimed responsibility in a telephone call to the press, Al Jazeera reported. The BBC said that a Taliban spokesman had said the group carried out the attack. Interior and defence ministry officials told the BBC, however, that the attack bore the hallmarks of the Haqqani network, a group closely allied with the Taliban that operates with some independence.

The Long War Journal reported that ISAF had said the attack was carried out "in conjunction with Taliban operatives", and it described a loose grouping it called the Kabul Attack Network, made up of Taliban, Haqqani and Hizb-i-Islami Gulbuddin fighters. According to the same report, ISAF said that Ismail Jan, a Haqqani commander operating in Paktia province, had provided "material support" for the attack. ISAF said a precision airstrike killed him in the Gardez district on 29 June. The report relied on ISAF's announcement, and no independent confirmation of his death is reported.

The motive is not settled in the reporting. Al Jazeera's account noted that the attack came as Afghan forces were preparing to take over security, and VOA said the Taliban appeared to want to show it could still carry out such assaults despite heavy operations against it. The Sydney Morning Herald called sowing doubt "clearly the intent of the Taliban". President Hamid Karzai, as the BBC reported, said the insurgents enjoyed spilling innocent blood but that the attack would not hinder the transfer of security responsibility to Afghan forces.

The US State Department spokeswoman, Victoria Nuland, said the United States "strongly condemns the attack on the Intercontinental Hotel in Kabul", adding that it showed the terrorists' disregard for human life. She said that all American embassy staff were accounted for. The US special representative for Afghanistan and Pakistan, Marc Grossman, had left Kabul hours before the attack. A State Department official told ABC News that no American officials had been affected, and ISAF said it had offered assistance to Afghan authorities.

Afghan officials insisted the plans would go ahead. VOA reported that Karzai said the attack would not stop Afghan forces from taking over their security role as planned, and that seven areas were due to be handed over the following month. The Afghan National Security Directorate spokesman, Mashal, said an investigation would definitely take place. The Sydney Morning Herald quoted a Western official who said the attack "introduces doubt": if the transition was to be based on security conditions, the conditions had not yet been met.

All of the attackers died during the assault.The most concrete follow-up in the early coverage concerns the Haqqani commander Ismail Jan. The Long War Journal reported ISAF's account that a special operations airstrike in Gardez killed him, and that ISAF said he had given "material support" to the attackers. Afghan officials, meanwhile, had acknowledged that a loophole in security existed.

The Inter-Continental was attacked again in January 2018. RFE/RL reported that a Taliban assault that began on 20 January that year, by militants dressed in army uniforms, had killed at least 30 people by one senior Afghan security official's count, with 14 foreigners among the dead. That attack was separate from the 2011 one, although RFE/RL's report noted that the hotel had been targeted in the June 2011 suicide attack that killed 21 people, including at least 10 civilians.
